overview: The OR operator is a logical operator in SQL that combines two or more boolean conditions and evaluates to TRUE when at least one of the conditions is TRUE.
It is used in the WHERE clause, JOIN ... ON clauses, HAVING clauses, and CHECK constraints to widen result sets so a row qualifies if any of several criteria is met.
OR has lower precedence than AND, follows SQL's three-valued logic (TRUE/FALSE/UNKNOWN), and has important index-usage and performance characteristics that distinguish it from IN.
learningObjectives: Understand how OR combines conditions, its truth table, and how it behaves with NULL under three-valued logic.
Master operator precedence (AND binds tighter than OR) and why parentheses are essential when mixing them.
Learn the relationship between OR and IN and the performance/index implications of OR predicates.
coreConcept.formalDefinition: OR is a binary logical disjunction operator that takes two boolean expressions and returns TRUE if at least one operand is TRUE; it returns FALSE only when both operands are FALSE, and UNKNOWN otherwise (per SQL's three-valued logic). In a WHERE clause, a row is returned only when the overall predicate evaluates to TRUE.
coreConcept.simpleExplanation: Think of OR as a lenient gatekeeper that lets a row through if it meets any one of the listed requirements. If you ask for customers who are 'in California' OR 'have spent over $1000', a row qualifies if either is true, even if the other is false.
coreConcept.historicalContext: OR derives from Boolean algebra (George Boole, 1854) and predicate logic, where it represents inclusive disjunction. SQL adopted AND, OR, and NOT as core logical connectives from its earliest standardization (SQL-86) and formalized their interaction with NULL through three-valued logic in later ANSI/ISO standards.

whyItMatters.business: OR lets analysts capture broader audiences or events (e.g., customers in any of several regions, or transactions flagged by any of several rules). Misusing OR or its precedence can wrongly include or exclude segments, distorting campaigns and reports.
whyItMatters.engineering: OR expresses alternatives declaratively, but it can defeat single-index access paths, so engineers must understand when an OR is index-friendly (via index merge / OR-to-UNION rewrites) and when it forces scans.
whyItMatters.scalability: OR predicates across different columns often prevent a single composite index from being used, which can cause full scans on large tables; recognizing this lets engineers rewrite to UNION or use index-merge strategies to scale.
whyItMatters.cost: Unoptimized OR predicates that trigger full scans increase CPU, I/O, and bytes-scanned cost in cloud warehouses. Rewriting OR to IN or UNION ALL where appropriate can substantially cut cost.
whyItMatters.reliability: Predictable disjunction semantics, including correct NULL/UNKNOWN handling, keep filters from silently including or dropping unexpected rows, which is essential for trustworthy results.

coreComponents.name: Boolean Operands (Alternatives)
coreComponents.definition: Each side of an OR is a condition that evaluates to TRUE, FALSE, or UNKNOWN, representing one acceptable alternative.
coreComponents.purpose: To express an individual sufficient condition; satisfying any one is enough.
coreComponents.responsibilities: Produce a three-valued boolean result for OR to disjunct; comparisons with NULL yield UNKNOWN.

coreComponents.name: The OR Connective
coreComponents.definition: The logical disjunction operator placed between two boolean operands, e.g., condition1 OR condition2.
coreComponents.purpose: To require that at least one of the combined conditions be TRUE for a row to qualify.
coreComponents.responsibilities: Apply the disjunction truth table; return TRUE if either side is TRUE, FALSE only if both are FALSE, otherwise UNKNOWN.

coreComponents.name: Evaluation Context (WHERE / ON / HAVING / CHECK)
coreComponents.definition: The clause in which the OR-combined predicate is evaluated, determining how TRUE/FALSE/UNKNOWN is applied.
coreComponents.purpose: To filter rows, match join partners, filter groups, or validate constraints based on the disjunction result.
coreComponents.responsibilities: In WHERE/ON/HAVING only rows where the predicate is TRUE are kept; in a CHECK constraint a row is rejected only when the predicate is FALSE (UNKNOWN passes).
coreComponents.examples: WHERE a OR b; HAVING SUM(x) > 100 OR COUNT(*) = 0; CHECK (type = 'A' OR type = 'B')

internalWorking: The parser builds an expression tree honoring precedence: NOT binds tightest, then AND, then OR; so 'a OR b AND c' parses as 'a OR (b AND c)'.

The optimizer may rewrite an OR on the same column into an IN list, or rewrite OR across different indexed columns into a UNION/index-merge plan; otherwise it may resort to a full scan because a single B-tree seek cannot satisfy disjoint ranges.

For each row, the engine evaluates operands and applies the OR truth table; if any operand is TRUE the result is TRUE regardless of the others, allowing the engine to stop evaluating remaining operands (when it chooses to short-circuit).
coreConcept.architectureFlow: Row source -> evaluate predicate tree (NOT, then AND, then OR) per row -> OR disjunction (TRUE if any operand TRUE) -> keep row only if overall result is TRUE -> output
dataFlowWalkthrough: 1. A query 'SELECT * FROM customers WHERE region = ''US'' OR region = ''CA''' is submitted.
2. The optimizer recognizes both predicates target the same column and may rewrite to region IN ('US','CA'), enabling a single index range/seek.
3. For each row it evaluates region = 'US'; if TRUE the OR is TRUE and the row is kept without evaluating the second operand.
4. If the first is FALSE, it evaluates region = 'CA'; the row is kept if that is TRUE. If region is NULL both comparisons are UNKNOWN, the OR is UNKNOWN, and the row is excluded.

keyTerminology.meaning: The logical OR operation that yields TRUE when at least one operand is TRUE (inclusive OR).
keyTerminology.importance: It is the formal name for OR and underpins how alternative filters are combined.

keyTerminology.meaning: SQL's OR is inclusive: TRUE OR TRUE is TRUE. Exclusive OR (XOR, true if exactly one is true) is not a standard SQL keyword and must be emulated.
keyTerminology.importance: Candidates must know SQL OR is inclusive, and that XOR is expressed with <> on booleans or CASE logic.

keyTerminology.meaning: Optimizer techniques that satisfy OR predicates by combining multiple index accesses or rewriting OR to UNION.
keyTerminology.importance: Explains when OR can still use indexes instead of forcing a full table scan.

importantConcepts.explanation: OR has the lowest precedence of the three logical operators. 'a OR b AND c' means 'a OR (b AND c)'. To force the OR to be grouped first, use parentheses: '(a OR b) AND c'.

TRUE OR UNKNOWN = TRUE, FALSE OR UNKNOWN = UNKNOWN, UNKNOWN OR UNKNOWN = UNKNOWN. A definite TRUE on one side makes the whole OR TRUE even if the other side is unknown; otherwise UNKNOWN propagates and the row is excluded by WHERE.

Multiple equality ORs on the same column (col = 'a' OR col = 'b' OR col = 'c') are equivalent to col IN ('a','b','c'). IN is more concise, easier to optimize, and avoids precedence mistakes, so it is generally preferred for value lists on a single column.

variationsAndTypes: **Same-column OR (equivalent to IN):** col = 'a' OR col = 'b', best rewritten as col IN ('a','b').
**Cross-column OR:** colA = x OR colB = y, which often defeats a single composite index and may need index merge or UNION.
**OR with range predicates:** amount < 10 OR amount > 1000, expressing disjoint ranges that a single seek cannot cover.
advantages: **Flexible Inclusion:** Captures rows meeting any of several alternatives, widening result sets as needed.
**Expressive:** Combines naturally with AND and NOT (with parentheses) to model complex business rules.
**Readable Alternatives:** Clearly states the acceptable options for a column or set of columns.
**Rewriteable:** Same-column ORs can be simplified to IN, and cross-column ORs can sometimes be turned into UNION for performance.
disadvantages: **Index Defeating:** Cross-column or disjoint-range ORs often prevent efficient single-index seeks, leading to scans.
**Precedence Confusion:** Because AND binds tighter, missing parentheses around an OR group is a frequent source of bugs.
**Over-Inclusion:** Adding OR alternatives can unintentionally widen results far beyond intent.
**NULL Subtleties:** FALSE OR UNKNOWN stays UNKNOWN, which WHERE treats as not-TRUE, so nullable operands need care.

tradeOffs.whenToUse: Use OR when a row should qualify if it meets any of several alternative conditions, such as multiple acceptable statuses, regions, or risk flags.
tradeOffs.whenToAvoid: Avoid OR for many equality values on one column (use IN), and be cautious with cross-column ORs on large tables where they cause scans; consider UNION ALL of indexed sub-queries instead.

coreConcept.realWorldAnalogy: OR is like a discount that applies if you are a student OR a senior OR a member. Meeting any one qualification gets you the discount; you do not need all of them. The more qualifying categories you add, the more people become eligible.

commonMisconceptions.myth: 'WHERE a = 1 OR a = 2 AND b = 3' returns rows where (a is 1 or 2) and b is 3.
commonMisconceptions.reality: AND binds tighter than OR, so it actually means 'a = 1 OR (a = 2 AND b = 3)'. To get the assumed meaning you must write '(a = 1 OR a = 2) AND b = 3'.

commonMisconceptions.myth: OR always prevents index usage, so it is inherently slow.
commonMisconceptions.reality: Same-column ORs become IN and use indexes well, and optimizers can use index merge or rewrite cross-column ORs to UNION. OR is only problematic when no such plan applies, forcing a scan.

productionConsiderations.scalability: Cross-column OR predicates on large tables can force full scans; scaling them often means rewriting to UNION ALL of two indexed queries or relying on index-merge plans. Same-column ORs scale well as IN-style index seeks.
productionConsiderations.reliability: Deterministic disjunction semantics make OR filters reproducible. Standardizing NULL handling keeps OR-based inclusion consistent across nullable columns.
productionConsiderations.faultTolerance: OR is a stateless per-row evaluation, so it produces identical results on retries, replicas, and after failover.
productionConsiderations.monitoring: Watch execution plans for OR predicates degrading to full scans; track query latency for OR-heavy filters and compare IN/UNION rewrites.
productionConsiderations.security: OR is a vector for SQL injection (e.g., appended '... OR 1=1' to bypass a filter). Always parameterize user input and never concatenate raw OR clauses from user data.
productionConsiderations.costOptimization: In bytes-scanned billing, OR predicates that prevent partition pruning increase cost; ensure partition columns are filtered with AND, and prefer IN/UNION rewrites that preserve pruning.
productionConsiderations.performance: Prefer IN over same-column OR, consider UNION ALL for cross-column OR on large tables, and keep operands sargable so index merge can apply.

codeExamples.title: Basic OR and its IN equivalent
codeExamples.overview: Selecting customers in any of several regions using OR, then showing the cleaner IN form.
codeExamples.code:
-- Using OR on the same column
SELECT customer_id, name, region
FROM customers
WHERE region = 'US' OR region = 'CA' OR region = 'MX';

-- Equivalent, cleaner, and easier to optimize
SELECT customer_id, name, region
FROM customers
WHERE region IN ('US', 'CA', 'MX');
codeExamples.breakdown: Both queries return the same rows: customers whose region is any of US, CA, or MX. IN is shorthand for chained same-column equality ORs and is generally preferred for readability and optimization.
codeExamples.expectedOutput: All customers located in the US, Canada, or Mexico; customers in any other region are excluded.
codeExamples.commonIssues: Forgetting that NULL region is excluded (NULL = 'US' is UNKNOWN), and accidentally mixing OR with an AND condition without parentheses.
codeExamples.optimizationTips: Use IN instead of multiple same-column ORs; an index on region serves the IN list as a set of range seeks.

codeExamples.title: Precedence: parentheses around an OR group
codeExamples.overview: Showing how AND binding tighter than OR changes results, and how to fix it with parentheses.
codeExamples.breakdown: In the first query every row with a = 1 qualifies regardless of b, plus rows where a = 2 and b = 3. The second restricts both a-values to rows where b = 3. The grouping changes the result set entirely.
codeExamples.expectedOutput: First query: all a = 1 rows plus a = 2 AND b = 3 rows. Second query: rows where a is 1 or 2 and b equals 3.
codeExamples.commonIssues: Assuming OR groups left-to-right with AND; this is the single most common OR/AND precedence bug.
codeExamples.optimizationTips: Always parenthesize OR groups when mixing with AND, for both correctness and clarity.

codeExamples.title: Rewriting a cross-column OR to UNION ALL for index usage
codeExamples.overview: A cross-column OR can force a scan; splitting into a UNION of two indexed lookups can be faster on large tables.
codeExamples.code:
-- Cross-column OR may not use a single index efficiently
SELECT order_id, customer_id, email
FROM orders
WHERE customer_id = 12345 OR email = 'jane@example.com';

-- Rewritten as UNION of two index-friendly queries
SELECT order_id, customer_id, email FROM orders WHERE customer_id = 12345
UNION
SELECT order_id, customer_id, email FROM orders WHERE email = 'jane@example.com';
codeExamples.breakdown: The OR version asks the optimizer to satisfy two predicates on different columns at once, which a single B-tree index cannot do; it may scan. The UNION version lets each branch use its own index (on customer_id and on email), and UNION removes duplicates that satisfy both.
codeExamples.expectedOutput: Both forms return orders matching either the customer_id or the email; the UNION form is typically faster when both columns are indexed and the table is large.
codeExamples.commonIssues: Using UNION ALL would duplicate rows that match both predicates; use UNION to dedupe, or add a guard to avoid double counting.
codeExamples.optimizationTips: Verify with EXPLAIN that the UNION branches use index seeks. If the optimizer already does index merge for the OR, the rewrite may be unnecessary.

endToEndExample.businessProblem: A support team needs to find all tickets that are either high priority OR have been open more than 7 days OR were escalated, so none of these at-risk tickets slip through. A ticket qualifies if any single condition holds.
endToEndExample.inputData: A tickets table with columns: ticket_id, priority ('low','medium','high'), created_at, status, is_escalated (boolean), and a nullable resolved_at.
endToEndExample.architecture: A relational table queried with an OR-combined WHERE clause, with supporting indexes on priority, created_at, and is_escalated to allow index-merge or UNION strategies.
processingSteps: 2. OR identify long-open tickets: created_at < CURRENT_DATE - INTERVAL '7' DAY AND resolved_at IS NULL.
3. OR identify escalated tickets: is_escalated = TRUE.
4. Group each multi-part alternative with parentheses so AND/OR precedence is correct.
5. The optimizer uses index merge across the indexed columns, or the query is rewritten as a UNION of three indexed branches for very large tables.
endToEndExample.output: A complete list of at-risk tickets where any one of the three conditions is satisfied, deduplicated so a ticket matching multiple conditions appears once.
endToEndExample.monitoring: Track the at-risk count daily; an unexpected jump can indicate a precedence bug widening the OR, while a drop to zero can indicate a NULL or AND interaction over-restricting an alternative. Review the plan for scans vs index merge.
endToEndExample.errorHandling: Validate parentheses in the dynamic filter builder; ensure each OR alternative that contains an AND (the long-open branch) is fully parenthesized so it does not leak unintended rows.
endToEndExample.finalResult: Support reliably surfaces every at-risk ticket because OR includes a ticket meeting any single criterion, while parentheses and NULL handling keep the multi-part alternatives correct.

industryUseCases.problem: Surfacing tickets that need attention for any of several reasons.
industryUseCases.solution: WHERE priority = 'high' OR is_escalated = TRUE OR (created_at < NOW() - INTERVAL '7 day' AND resolved_at IS NULL) combines alternatives with OR.
industryUseCases.benefits: Ensures no at-risk ticket is missed regardless of which single condition triggers it, improving SLA compliance.

industryUseCases.problem: Building broad audience segments from multiple acceptable attributes.
industryUseCases.solution: WHERE country IN ('US','CA','UK') OR lifetime_value > 5000 includes anyone in target geographies or any high-value customer.
industryUseCases.benefits: Reaches all relevant prospects with one query; IN handles the geography list efficiently while OR adds the value-based alternative.

industryUseCases.company: Security and Fraud Monitoring (e.g., Cloudflare, Datadog)
industryUseCases.problem: Alerting when any of several independent risk signals fires.
industryUseCases.solution: WHERE failed_logins > 10 OR ip_reputation = 'bad' OR is_new_device = TRUE flags events matching any single rule.
industryUseCases.benefits: Catches threats triggered by any individual signal, maximizing detection coverage while rules remain individually tunable.

productionDeepDive.scalability: OR scalability hinges on index strategy: same-column ORs scale as IN-based index seeks, but cross-column or disjoint-range ORs may force scans. For very large tables, rewriting OR to UNION ALL of indexed branches (with dedupe where needed) restores scalable access paths.
productionDeepDive.faultTolerance: OR predicates are deterministic and stateless per row, producing identical results on retries, replicas, and after failover, supporting idempotent reprocessing.
productionDeepDive.highAvailability: OR filtering is pure computation over inputs and behaves identically across read replicas; only replication lag (data freshness) affects results, not the operator itself.
productionDeepDive.disasterRecovery: OR-filtered queries are fully reproducible from restored data with no operator-specific state to recover; re-running yields the same result for the same data.
productionDeepDive.performanceOptimization: Prefer IN over same-column ORs, use UNION ALL/UNION for cross-column ORs when index merge is not chosen, keep operands sargable, and verify plans with EXPLAIN to confirm index usage rather than scans.
productionDeepDive.costOptimization: In bytes-scanned engines, ensure partition-pruning columns are filtered with AND outside the OR; OR predicates that block pruning can multiply scanned data. Rewrites to IN or UNION can restore pruning and cut cost.
productionDeepDive.securityConsiderations: OR is the canonical SQL-injection bypass (appended OR 1=1). Always use parameterized queries and never build OR clauses by concatenating untrusted input; validate any dynamic column allowlists.
productionDeepDive.monitoringAndObservability: Capture and diff query plans for OR-heavy queries; alert when an index-merge plan regresses to a full scan, which often follows a schema or statistics change.
productionDeepDive.dataQualityValidation: Use OR in CHECK constraints to allow enumerated valid states, e.g., CHECK (type = 'A' OR type = 'B' OR type = 'C'), though IN is usually clearer.
productionDeepDive.loggingAndAlerting: Log cardinality of OR-filtered alerts/segments; sharp changes can indicate a precedence bug or an over-broad OR alternative that needs review.

recommendedPractices: **Prefer IN over multiple same-column ORs** for readability, fewer precedence mistakes, and better optimization.
**Parenthesize OR groups** whenever mixing with AND, since AND binds tighter than OR.
**Consider UNION ALL/UNION for cross-column ORs** on large tables to enable per-branch index usage.
**Handle NULL operands explicitly** so FALSE OR UNKNOWN does not silently exclude rows you expected.
engineeringStandards: Compound predicates mixing AND and OR must use explicit parentheses; ambiguous mixes should fail code review.
Same-column equality lists must use IN rather than chained OR unless there is a documented reason.
Cross-column OR predicates on large tables must be reviewed for plan quality and rewritten if they cause full scans.
designRecommendations: Model enumerable valid states so OR/IN lists stay short and indexable.
Add indexes on each column referenced by cross-column ORs so index-merge or UNION branches can seek.
Avoid disjoint-range ORs on hot paths; consider precomputed flags or partitioning to support them.
namingConventions: Use is_/has_ prefixes for boolean alternatives so OR conditions read naturally (e.g., is_escalated OR is_flagged).
Name CHECK constraints with enumerated OR/IN options descriptively, e.g., chk_ticket_valid_priority.
documentationStandards: Document the intended grouping of any OR/AND mix next to the query.
Record whether cross-column ORs are served by index merge or a UNION rewrite, and why.
Note NULL-handling decisions for OR alternatives on nullable columns.
testingStrategies: Test each OR branch independently and in combination to confirm coverage and dedupe behavior.
Include rows with NULLs in OR operands to verify three-valued logic behavior.
Compare OR vs IN vs UNION rewrites for both result equality and execution plan quality.

commonMistakes.mistake: Forgetting parentheses when mixing OR with AND.
commonMistakes.whyItHappens: Developers assume left-to-right evaluation and overlook that AND binds tighter than OR.
commonMistakes.impact: The query silently returns the wrong rows, e.g., all a = 1 rows leak in regardless of the AND condition.
commonMistakes.correctApproach: Wrap OR groups: WHERE (a = 1 OR a = 2) AND b = 3.

commonMistakes.mistake: Using many same-column ORs instead of IN.
commonMistakes.whyItHappens: Habit or unfamiliarity with IN; building predicates programmatically.
commonMistakes.impact: Verbose, error-prone predicates that are harder to optimize and more likely to hide precedence bugs.
commonMistakes.correctApproach: Rewrite col = 'a' OR col = 'b' OR col = 'c' as col IN ('a','b','c').

commonMistakes.mistake: Cross-column OR forcing a full table scan on a large table.
commonMistakes.whyItHappens: Assuming OR uses indexes the same way AND does, without checking the plan.
commonMistakes.impact: Severe latency and cost as the engine scans the whole table to satisfy disjoint single-column predicates.
commonMistakes.correctApproach: Verify with EXPLAIN; rewrite to UNION/UNION ALL of indexed branches or ensure index-merge is available.

comparisonSection.explanation: OR has lower precedence than AND, so 'a OR b AND c' is 'a OR (b AND c)'. OR widens results (any condition sufficient) while AND narrows them (all conditions required). Mixing them safely requires parentheses around the OR group.

They are logically equivalent for equality on the same column, but IN is more concise, less error-prone with precedence, and typically easier for the optimizer to turn into efficient index range seeks. Prefer IN for value lists.

comparisonSection.optionA: OR across columns (colA = x OR colB = y)
comparisonSection.explanation: A cross-column OR often cannot use a single index and may scan, whereas splitting into UNION lets each branch use its own index. UNION dedupes overlapping matches; UNION ALL is faster but keeps duplicates that satisfy both predicates.

beginnerQuestions.question: What does the OR operator do and when does it return TRUE?
beginnerQuestions.answer: OR combines conditions and returns TRUE when at least one condition is TRUE. In a WHERE clause it returns rows that satisfy any of the conditions, widening the result set; it returns FALSE only when all conditions are FALSE.
beginnerQuestions.explanation: State the inclusive disjunction truth table and contrast with AND. Mention it broadens results.

beginnerQuestions.question: How is OR related to the IN operator?
beginnerQuestions.answer: A series of equality ORs on the same column is equivalent to IN. For example, region = 'US' OR region = 'CA' OR region = 'MX' is the same as region IN ('US','CA','MX'). IN is shorter and easier to optimize.
beginnerQuestions.explanation: This tests recognition of the OR/IN equivalence and the preference for IN on single-column value lists.

intermediateQuestions.question: Why is 'WHERE a = 1 OR a = 2 AND b = 3' often a bug?
intermediateQuestions.answer: Because AND binds tighter than OR, it is parsed as 'a = 1 OR (a = 2 AND b = 3)'. So every row with a = 1 qualifies regardless of b. The likely intended query is '(a = 1 OR a = 2) AND b = 3'.
intermediateQuestions.explanation: Demonstrate the precedence rule and the parenthesized fix; this is a classic interview trap.

intermediateQuestions.question: How does OR behave with NULL values?
intermediateQuestions.answer: Comparisons with NULL yield UNKNOWN. TRUE OR UNKNOWN is TRUE, FALSE OR UNKNOWN is UNKNOWN, and UNKNOWN OR UNKNOWN is UNKNOWN. Since WHERE keeps only TRUE rows, an OR that resolves to UNKNOWN excludes the row.
intermediateQuestions.explanation: Walk the 3VL truth table for OR; emphasize that a single TRUE branch rescues the row but otherwise UNKNOWN excludes it.

advancedQuestions.question: Why can an OR across two different columns hurt performance, and how do you fix it?
advancedQuestions.answer: A single B-tree index can satisfy one column's predicate, not two disjoint ones at once, so a cross-column OR may force a full scan. Fixes include relying on the optimizer's index-merge plan, or rewriting the OR as a UNION (to dedupe) of two queries each using its own index.
advancedQuestions.explanation: Tests understanding of why disjunction defeats single-index seeks and the UNION/index-merge remedies; mention verifying with EXPLAIN.

advancedQuestions.question: Is SQL's OR inclusive or exclusive, and how would you implement exclusive OR (XOR)?
advancedQuestions.answer: SQL OR is inclusive: TRUE OR TRUE is TRUE. There is no standard XOR keyword. You can emulate XOR with '(a OR b) AND NOT (a AND b)', or for booleans with 'a <> b', or via CASE expressions.
advancedQuestions.explanation: Tests precise knowledge that OR is inclusive and the ability to derive XOR from primitives.

scenarioBasedQuestions.scenario: A query 'WHERE customer_id = 123 OR email = ''x@y.com''' is slow on a 500M-row orders table even though both columns are indexed. How do you speed it up?
scenarioBasedQuestions.thinkingProcess: Recognize that a cross-column OR may not use either index in a single seek, causing a scan. Consider index merge availability; if not used, rewrite to UNION of two index-seek queries and dedupe.
scenarioBasedQuestions.expectedAnswer: Rewrite as 'SELECT ... WHERE customer_id = 123 UNION SELECT ... WHERE email = ''x@y.com''' so each branch uses its index, and UNION removes rows matching both. Confirm with EXPLAIN that both branches seek.

systemDesignQuestions.problemStatement: Design a flexible search endpoint that lets users match records by any of several optional filters (name, email, phone, or external_id). How do you keep it correct, secure, and fast?
systemDesignQuestions.designApproach: Build the predicate as a parenthesized OR of only the filters the user supplied, each parameterized. For large tables, generate a UNION of index-seek sub-queries (one per supplied filter) rather than a single cross-column OR.
systemDesignQuestions.tradeOffs: A single OR query is simpler to build but may scan; the UNION approach is faster but more code and needs dedupe. Allowing arbitrary OR filters increases flexibility but risks non-sargable predicates; restrict to indexed columns.
systemDesignQuestions.scalingStrategy: Index every searchable column, generate one UNION branch per active filter so each uses its index, cap the number of OR alternatives, and keep mandatory tenant/partition predicates as AND to preserve pruning.

followUpQuestions: When is it safe to use UNION ALL instead of UNION when rewriting an OR?
How does the optimizer's index-merge feature relate to manually rewriting OR as UNION?
What is the precedence of NOT relative to AND and OR?
How would you express 'exactly one of a or b is true' in standard SQL?
Why might 'col = NULL OR col = 'x'' miss the NULL rows, and how do you fix it?

cheatSheet.oneLineDefinition: OR is the logical disjunction operator that returns TRUE when at least one combined condition is TRUE, widening the result set.
keyConcepts: Disjunction: TRUE if any operand TRUE (inclusive OR).
Precedence: NOT > AND > OR; parenthesize OR groups.
Three-valued logic: TRUE OR UNKNOWN = TRUE, FALSE OR UNKNOWN = UNKNOWN.
OR vs IN: same-column equality ORs equal IN; prefer IN.
Index usage: cross-column ORs may scan; use UNION/index merge.
commands: SELECT * FROM t WHERE region = 'US' OR region = 'CA';
SELECT * FROM t WHERE region IN ('US','CA','MX');
SELECT * FROM t WHERE (a = 1 OR a = 2) AND b = 3;
SELECT * FROM t WHERE col_a = 1 UNION SELECT * FROM t WHERE col_b = 2;
interviewPoints: OR is inclusive; XOR is not a standard keyword.
AND binds tighter than OR; always parenthesize.
Cross-column OR can force scans; use UNION/index merge.
FALSE OR UNKNOWN stays UNKNOWN; WHERE excludes it.
quickNotes: Use IN for value lists on one column instead of chained OR.
Parenthesize every OR group when mixing with AND.
Verify OR plans with EXPLAIN; watch for full scans.
Rewrite cross-column OR to UNION (dedupe) or UNION ALL (faster, dupes).
Never concatenate user input into OR clauses; parameterize to prevent injection.

keyTakeaways: OR returns TRUE when at least one condition is TRUE, so it widens result sets and is the right choice when any of several alternatives should qualify a row.
Operator precedence is NOT > AND > OR; because OR is lowest, mixed expressions must parenthesize the OR group to avoid the most common SQL logic bug.
A list of equality ORs on the same column is equivalent to IN, which is more concise, less error-prone, and usually easier for the optimizer to serve with an index.
Cross-column or disjoint-range ORs often defeat single-index seeks and can force full scans; rewriting to UNION of indexed branches or relying on index merge restores performance.
Under three-valued logic, TRUE OR UNKNOWN is TRUE but FALSE OR UNKNOWN is UNKNOWN, so OR operands on nullable columns need explicit NULL handling to avoid silently excluding rows.
